snip.t: Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) plan in response to COVID-19
Driven by: antibiotic overuse/misuse, incomplete courses, agricultural use, poor infection prevention and control
Infection prevention and control (IPC) — hand hygiene, PPE, isolation of resistant organisms

es.q: Outline the Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) facility preparedness requirements in response to COVID-19.
es.m:
- **IPC program**: Facilities must have an IPC program or a dedicated IPC focal person.
- **Triage and screening**: A functional screening and triage area for early case identification is required.
- **Holding area**: A designated holding area for cases awaiting results or transfer must be established.
- **Precautions**: Mechanisms must be in place to ensure standard and transmission-based precautions.
- **Staffing and training**: Adequate healthcare workers to provide 24-hour care without exhaustion, continuous training/refresher courses, and a health worker exposure risk assessment plan.
- **Supplies**: Facilities must maintain adequate IPC supplies and equipment.

faq.a: Hand hygiene stops transmission at the source, reducing the need for antibiotics and limiting resistance.
faq.q: Why is hand hygiene more effective than antibiotics in preventing HAIs?

faq.a: Yes, if they are washed at ≥80 °C after each use and stored clean; they must be changed between patients.
faq.q: Can cloth gowns be used safely when disposable PPE is unavailable?

faq.a: Notify infection control, review operative sterility practices, and isolate affected patients while the source is investigated.
faq.q: What is the first step when a cluster of surgical site infections is identified?

exam: What immediate IPC measure should you implement for a patient with suspected multidrug‑resistant TB on a crowded ward? — Place the patient in a separate, well‑ventilated area, use N95 respirators for staff, and enforce strict hand hygiene.
How would you modify hand‑hygiene practice when running water is unavailable? — Provide alcohol‑based hand rub (≥60 % ethanol) at each bedside and train staff on its correct use.

A surgeon reports an increase in post‑operative wound infections; what IPC audit would you prioritize? — Conduct a peri‑operative checklist audit focusing on instrument sterilisation and intra‑operative glove changes.

Why is chlorhexidine preferred over plain soap for surgical site preparation in low‑resource settings? — Chlorhexidine has persistent antimicrobial activity, reducing skin flora for longer periods, and is inexpensive.
During a COVID‑19 surge, PPE supplies are limited; what reusable option can be safely employed? — Use autoclave‑compatible gowns and face shields that can be disinfected between uses.

Explain the difference between contact and droplet precautions and give an example of each common in East Africa. — Contact: gloves and gown for MRSA or ESBL; Droplet: surgical mask for pertussis or influenza.

A patient develops a catheter‑associated urinary tract infection; what IPC steps stop further cases? — Remove unnecessary catheters, enforce aseptic insertion technique, and maintain closed drainage systems.

How does antimicrobial stewardship support IPC, and why must both be present in a hospital plan? — Stewardship reduces selective pressure for resistant organisms, decreasing the burden on IPC to control spread.
ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: A practical guide for clinicians in East African and similar settings to apply infection prevention and control (IPC) at the bedside and on the ward, focusing on common local pathogens and limited diagnostics.

b: Hand hygiene failure
Improper use of personal protective equipment (PPE)
Inadequate cleaning of surfaces or equipment
Failure to isolate patients with known or suspected transmissible infections
sections.p: IPC is the set of evidence‑based measures that prevent transmission of infectious agents within health‑care facilities. Diagnosis is clinical – recognising a breach in practice that could spread pathogens.

b: Low: no known colonised patient, standard precautions sufficient
Moderate: colonised patient present, need contact or droplet precautions
High: outbreak, need cohorting, enhanced environmental cleaning, and possible facility lockdown
sections.p: IPC breaches are graded by risk to patients and staff: low (routine care), moderate (potential exposure to multidrug‑resistant organisms), high (known outbreak or exposure to highly transmissible agents such as Ebola, COVID‑19).

b: Hand‑contamination due to lack of running water or alcohol‑based hand rub
Reuse or improper sterilisation of equipment (e.g., syringes, surgical instruments)
Crowded wards and inadequate ventilation
Limited PPE supplies leading to reuse without proper decontamination
High prevalence of multidrug‑resistant bacteria (ESBL‑producing Enterobacteriaceae, MRSA) in the community
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals the most common drivers of infection spread are:

b: Fever > 38 °C after 48 h of admission without other source
Purulent wound drainage or cellulitis at a procedural site
New cough, dyspnoea, or infiltrates in a ventilated patient
sections.p: IPC failures are not a disease but become evident when patients develop health‑care associated infections (HAIs). Typical presentations include surgical site infection, catheter‑associated urinary tract infection, or ventilator‑associated pneumonia.
Investigations focus on identifying the pathogen and confirming the breach.

t.b: Is the infection bacterial and what morphology? → Guides empirical antibiotic choice
Which organism and its drug susceptibility? → Allows targeted therapy and informs outbreak control
Is the environment contaminated? → Triggers cleaning audit
Are staff performing hand hygiene? → Drives education and monitoring

t.a: If lab unavailable: bedside Gram‑stain or rapid antigen test (e.g., malaria, TB LAM)
t.b: Provides provisional organism clue → Allows provisional therapy while awaiting formal results

b: Cluster of >2 similar HAIs within 48 h
Rapid spread of multidrug‑resistant organism to multiple wards
High mortality among patients with ventilator‑associated pneumonia
Staff absenteeism due to occupational infection
sections.p: Failure to control infection can rapidly lead to outbreaks and severe patient harm.

b: Isolate or cohort patients with confirmed or suspected transmissible infection
Implement WHO ‘Five Moments for Hand Hygiene’; provide alcohol‑based rubs if water scarce
Use gloves, gowns, masks appropriate to transmission route; prioritize reusable PPE that can be autoclaved
Clean surfaces with chlorine‑based disinfectant (0.5 % for routine, 1 % for outbreak)
Treat infections with first‑line antibiotics per local formulary; avoid broad‑spectrum agents unless resistance documented
sections.p: IPC management combines immediate containment, treatment of infected patients, and system‑wide improvements.

b: Daily hand‑hygiene audit and feedback to staff
Monthly review of HAI rates and resistance patterns
Training sessions on proper PPE donning/doffing using locally available materials
Ensure supply chain for soap, alcohol rub, and disinfectant
Engage hospital leadership for policy support
sections.p: Sustained IPC requires monitoring, feedback, and adaptation to resource constraints.

b: IPC prevents spread; AMS optimises drug use. Both are complementary but distinct.
sections.p: IPC is sometimes mixed up with antimicrobial stewardship (AMS).

b: Prior antibiotic use can sterilise specimens, giving false‑negative cultures
Poor sample collection technique may miss organisms
Rapid antigen tests may have limited sensitivity for some bacteria
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, negative cultures do not rule out infection.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden rise in fever and sepsis among several patients on the same ward
Detection of a highly resistant organism (e.g., carbapenem‑resistant Enterobacteriaceae)
Outbreak of a viral haemorrhagic fever or COVID‑19 within the facility
